input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-243: The Mechanics of Programming. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Students will be introduced to the details of program structure and the mechanics of execution as well as supportive operating system features. Security and performance issues in program design will be discussed. The program translation process will be examined. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisite: C- or better in CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-243]
Students will be introduced to the details of program structure and the mechanics of execution as well as supportive operating system features. Security and performance issues in program design will be discussed. The program translation process will be examined. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisite: C- or better in CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Programs are organized into modules that define distinct units of code and data.
beats.example: A C program divides functionality into functions and global variables.
beats.title: Introduction to Program Structure
beats.visualDirection: Display a block diagram showing a main function calling three sub-functions with a shared data structure.

beats.claim: Execution follows a sequential flow controlled by conditional statements and loops.
beats.example: A for-loop iterates through an array, updating a running total each cycle.
beats.title: Execution Mechanics Overview
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart with a start node, a loop diamond, and exit arrows based on a boolean condition.

beats.claim: Variables occupy specific memory locations that the processor accesses during runtime.
beats.example: An integer variable stores a fixed-size binary representation in RAM.
beats.title: Memory Management Basics
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a memory map with labeled addresses, data types, and pointer offsets.

beats.claim: Source code undergoes compilation, linking, and assembly to produce an executable binary.
beats.example: A compiler translates C syntax into machine instructions for the target CPU architecture.
beats.title: Program Translation Process
beats.visualDirection: Present a pipeline diagram showing source code, preprocessor, compiler, linker, and final executable.

beats.claim: The operating system manages resource allocation and provides system calls for program execution.
beats.example: A file I/O operation requests disk access through an OS kernel interface.
beats.title: Operating System Integration
beats.visualDirection: Draw a layered diagram with application code, OS API, and kernel resource managers.

beats.claim: Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name.
beats.example: Using AES-256 with proper key management ensures confidentiality against known attacks.
beats.title: Security Design Principles
beats.visualDirection: Show a key lifecycle diagram covering generation, distribution, storage, and revocation.

beats.claim: Performance issues in program design require careful analysis of time and space complexity.
beats.example: Replacing nested loops with hash maps reduces average lookup time from O(n²) to O(1).
beats.title: Performance Optimization Strategies
beats.visualDirection: Display a comparison chart of algorithmic time complexity across different data structures.

beats.claim: Security requirements should be tracked throughout development to prevent vulnerabilities.
beats.example: Maintaining a threat model document updates trust boundaries as the codebase evolves.
beats.title: Secure Development Practices
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist template with fields for asset, threat, control, and residual risk.

beats.claim: Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed correctly.
beats.example: Static analysis tools scan source code for buffer overflows before compilation.
beats.title: Verification and Testing Methods
beats.visualDirection: Show a testing workflow diagram linking unit tests, integration tests, and security scans.

beats.claim: Program design must balance structure, execution efficiency, and security requirements.
beats.example: A secure, performant module validates inputs, manages memory safely, and follows established standards.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a three-column matrix evaluating code against structure, performance, and security criteria.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of program structure and execution mechanics.
Explain the program translation process from source code to executable binary.
Identify key security and performance considerations in program design.
